extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Renaissance intellectual history / biography of Erasmus
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly biographical chapter recounting Erasmus's methods, character, patronage-seeking, correspondence, and his first visit to England (1498–1500).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learned status based on published work, not bought title
rubrics_metrics.description: "In former times no one was called 'doctus' because he had bought the title of Doctor, but they were called Doctors who by putting forth books had given evident witness of their learning."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erasmus (as cited here) treats true scholarly distinction as earned by producing books that display learning rather than by purchasing or merely holding a formal degree; the passage criticises contemporary tendencies to value the formal title ('magister'/'doctor') over demonstrable published learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and classical command in languages (Latin and Greek)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good scholarship is described as "profound, exact and classic, both in Latin and in Greek."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplars given are Grocyn, Linacre, and Colet; the passage treats mastery of classical languages and exact, rigorous classical learning as core evaluative standards for humanist scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep learning connected with life and contemporary relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Learning, divorced from life, was already beginning to lose its hold upon many circles of European interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author (via Erasmus's perspective) treats an important quality criterion as the capacity of learning to engage with real life and modern concerns; purely pedantic or hair-splitting learning is criticized as losing public relevance and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly-method criterion: return to original texts and early commentators
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate rejection of the mediæval method by "going straight back, first to the original documents of Christianity themselves, and then to the early commentators... Jerome," aiming at new, scientific editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For theological scholarship and textual reform, the standard is philological: study original documents and authoritative early commentators to produce improved editions and clearer theological understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical guideline for securing patronage: preserve dignity and avoid appearing desperate
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus counsels delaying, raising his value in the patron's eyes, and not coming "flying at the first nod," arguing that one must not appear a 'greenhorn or a knave' or in 'the last extremity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics illustrated in the letters: do not reveal extreme need; frame requests so as to increase perceived worth; use a trusted intermediary (Battus) to press the case; demand reasonable travel allowance and convey expectations (horses, servant) rather than imploring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical composition of petitions: conceal requests within literary composition and flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: One letter is described as "really an essay in classical composition, with its object, the getting of money, partly concealed under the cover of literary digression."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective petitions combine fulsome eulogy and classical allusion with specific practical requests presented later; employ tasteful literary forms and learned references to flatter patrons while making explicit the financial needs and proposed returns (dedications, services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dedications, livings, and literary promises as currency for patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus sought concrete benefits (travel funds, horses, church livings) and relied on dedications and promise of learned works as the expected return for patronage: "payment for dedications."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page treats such exchanges as a normative practice: scholars should make explicit what they will produce (books, dedications, editions) in return for patronal support and may aim for enduring preferments (a church living) rather than one-off gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profile traits of a successful humanist scholar
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful humanists combine wide culture, mastery of classics, a broader outlook from travel (e.g., Italy), and the ability to connect antiquity with present religious and intellectual concerns (Colet described as like 'listening to Plato's self').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a composite evaluative standard: personal qualities (gentleness, character), cultivation (Italian journey, broad reading), skill (language mastery), and an orientation toward applying classical learning to contemporary theological and moral problems mark the effective humanist scholar.
